transcript:
User: Hello? Yeah... I got your card. You help with phones, right?
Agent: Yeah, we help with phones — got it. What about phones is giving you the most trouble right now?
User: Uh, calls going to voicemail... don't really track how many. Maybe ten? Fifteen? Hard to say exactly.
Agent: Mhm, makes sense — so some are hitting voicemail and it’s hard to know how many. When those calls go to voicemail now, what usually happens — do people wait for you to call back, or do they just move on to someone else?
User: Uh, not sure. Some wait, I think. Others might move on. Hard to tell.
Agent: Right, that uncertainty’s tough — you don’t really know which ones you’re losing. So on a typical day, is it mostly you handling the phone yourself, or do you have anyone dedicated to answering calls?
User: Uh, it's mostly me. I don't have anyone just for calls. Sometimes, I'm busy with the work outside.
Agent: Got it, so it’s mainly you and when you’re out working, the phone’s kind of on its own. When those 10–15 calls a day hit voicemail while you’re outside, what do you feel you’re most at risk of losing — new jobs, existing customers, or something else?
User: Uh, probably new jobs. Existing customers usually know how to reach me, but new ones might not wait.
Agent: Yeah, that makes sense — the new jobs are the ones that disappear when they hit voicemail. When someone calls you for the very first time and you miss it, do you usually see them try again, or is it more like that call just… vanishes?
User: Uh, they usually don't call back. I guess they just vanish.
Agent: Yeah… those first-time callers that just disappear, that’s exactly where the lost jobs sneak in. Given all that, are you actually looking for something that can step in and handle those calls when you’re out working, so those new jobs don’t vanish on you?
User: Uh, yeah, I think so. Having someone handle calls might help. Not sure how it all works, though.
Agent: Got it, that totally makes sense — and yeah, having “someone” there when you’re out is exactly what we focus on. Before I explain how it works, has anyone ever walked you through what those vanished calls are actually costing you in jobs and dollars?
User: Uh, no, not really. I never thought about it much. Costs? I guess it matters, right?
Agent: Yeah, it definitely matters — those “vanished” calls are usually the ones that turn into real jobs. Mind if we do a super quick ballpark on it together, just using your numbers? Takes like 30 seconds.
User: Uh, okay, we can try that. Not sure how it works, but I'm listening.
Agent: Perfect, thanks for rolling with me. So ballpark, just your best guess — in a typical week, how many calls do you think end up on voicemail instead of actually reaching you: more like 10, 20, 30?
User: Uh, I'd guess more like 10 or 15? Hard to be sure, though.
Agent: Got it, let’s use 15 to stay conservative. Of those missed calls, what percentage do you think would actually turn into a job if you picked up — maybe around half, like 50%, or would you put it higher or lower?
User: Uh, I have no idea. Maybe half? Could be more, but hard to say for sure.
Agent: Makes sense, we’ll stick with 50% to keep it simple. And what’s your average job worth for a new customer — are we talking more like $400, $650, $1,000?
Agent: Perfect, let’s use 650. So with your numbers, if you booked even 50% of those 15 missed calls, that’s about $4,875 extra a week — and over a month, roughly $21,100 — does that feel like it lines up with what you’re seeing, or is that a bit surprising?
User: Uh, depends, maybe four hundred? Or five? Not sure about higher amounts.
Agent: Got it, so even if we dial it down and say closer to four or five hundred a job, you’re still watching thousands walk away every month when those first-time callers vanish. Hearing that, does it make you more interested in having something in place that just catches every call and books the job while you’re out working?
User: Uh, yeah, sounds like it might be helpful, catching calls and booking while I'm busy.
Agent: Makes sense, that’s exactly what we set up — so, it’s a quick 20‑minute walkthrough where we show you how it would work on your phones and what those numbers look like with it on; what’s better for you for that live call, later today or sometime tomorrow?
User: Uh, maybe tomorrow? Need a bit of time to think about it. What time are you thinking?
Agent: Totally fair, tomorrow works and you can think on it a bit. Before we pick a time with Jay, can I grab your first name so I know who he’ll be speaking with?
User: Uh, it's Pedro. We'll see how this goes. What time do you think for tomorrow?
Agent: Nice to meet you, Pedro. Before we lock in a time with Jay tomorrow, what’s the name of your company?
User: Uh, it's just Pedro's Landscaping. Not much of a company name, just me mostly.
Agent: Got it, Pedro's Landscaping — that works. And… is the number you’re calling from right now the best number to reach you, or do you use a different one for business?
User: Uh, yeah, this number is fine. It's the one I use for work and everything.
Agent: Perfect, we’ll use this one. Quick check — are you on Eastern time where you are, or Central, Mountain, or Pacific?
Agent: Got it, we’ll stick with this number and you’re on Central. So for tomorrow, I can get you in around 1:00 or 1:45 in the afternoon — which of those works better for you?
User: Uh, I'm on Eastern time. That's the time zone here.
Agent: Ah, thanks for correcting that — we’ll use Eastern then. Oh sorry, I didn’t get your number quite right earlier — could you read me your cell number real quick, just so Jay can reach you for that call tomorrow?
User: Uh, sure, it's 555-123-4567. That's the number you can reach me on.
Agent: One moment while I confirm that.
Agent: One moment while I confirm that.
Agent: So Pedro, looks like the calendar’s giving us trouble locking that in for tomorrow at 1:00 Eastern, but I’ve got your number and we’ll give you a quick call within the hour to confirm that time. Is there anything else you need from me before I let you go for now?
